title: how are 2.5D indie devs and ai gamedevs generating isometric vector props without broken tile seams, 5,000 anchor points but also chatbot complications?
author: MaraVossk
selftext:
now building an isometric tactics prototype in Godot 4.3 using a standard 2:1 projection grid (64x32px base tiles), or rather compiling it all in godot while trying to generate a lot of assets via different methods.. so,   
  
I needed \~30 modular environmental props (military crates, generator hubs, blast doors, radio consoles) that match our clean vector/cel-shaded aesthetic   
  
tried the usual generative workflows and hit immediate engine blockers, but seems not to be good enough. what I will not probably use:  
1. Raster Diffusion (standard raster diffusion generators/diffusion models): The anti-aliased edges bleed background pixels into the texture atlas. When Godot renders the tiles under camera zoom, you get ugly 1px magenta/black seam artifacts along tile seams  
2. auto-tracing rasters (Illustrator / Inkscape): ok, this gives me too many nodes realistically (4,000+ tiny shards per crate). and building custom 2D collision polygons (\`CollisionPolygon2D\`) from auto-traced vectors takes longer than hand-drawing from scratch because you have to clean up hundreds of stray vertices  
3. stylistic perspective drift: Asset A is rendered at true 30degree isometric, but Asset B drifts into 45degr. dimetric perspective, making stacking props look visually broken.  
  
is there any AI tool that outputs real vectors with strict isometric constraint and clean bezier paths, or are you guys still hand-pulling every vertex in Aseprite/Illustrator? any tips or methods would be appreciated, and I don't want to compile it through usual chatbot or agent as I would like to be able to work with it in canvas/boards and edit in process, as a bit of a designer myself

comments.author: t-rook
comments.body: now tried to test 4 crates and a communications tower in recraft bc I often do gamedev and game podcast related stuff in recraft as a sort of 'design generator'. the isometric projection held true  angles  as i wanted them, quite consistantly, across all assets i done today. then I exported SVGs, opened in Inkscape to measure the footprint: bottom one of the items was an exact 2:1 ratio (width was precisely 2x the height), so similar to what you try to work out, then dropped into Godot 4.3 TileSet, snapped to grid cleanly with zero seam bleeding. testing animated sprite sheets next and if you got questions on the workflow, dm me

comments.author: Affectionate_Fact854
comments.body: Just make a 3d model , and render in isometric view using blender

replies.author: Mindestiny
replies.body: This is pretty much the industry answer.  Look at any isometric tactics game dating all the way back to Tactics ogre, FFT, etc.  Characters are 2D billboards, environments and doodads are 3D and the camera makes it isometric.

comments.author: CycleMother2006
comments.body:
Iso is hard even with human-driven workflows. One of two things happens:

1. A studio decides to create 3d models even for what is displaying as 2d iso, and rasterizes sprites at whatever angle they are choosing for their game. This is for maximum consistency, but fairly high tedium IMO and unless you have strong stylistic reasons, there isn't much reason to build in 3d just to use in 2d. You lose a lot of 2d flexibility here.

2. You go the Stardew Valley route. You stop caring if the angle of one prop you drew or generated matches the angle of another. Or if your barn matches the same angle as the general store. You visually gauge everything, and say, "It looks good, that's what matters." Because in reality, that's what people care about. Does it look good or feel off? Is it giving the information you want to provide?

The difficulty with #2 is either you or someone you're working with has to have a keen eye for what looks good. A lot of people simply don't have that.
